hero.text: Tens of thousands of orphans live in Israel. Mishpacha stands with them and their families, and builds the systems, knowledge and partnerships that change how the whole field responds – from personal mentoring to national policy.

about.title: Having their back – and changing the system around them
intro: Mishpacha was born from personal experience. Orphaned children, teens and young adults need real guidance in the most decisive years: adolescence, military service and the first steps into independent adulthood.

We're not another welfare body but a family that walks alongside them. Alongside personal support, we build knowledge, technology and partnerships with authorities and government ministries, so the response to orphans in Israel is clear, accessible and continuous.

pillars.title: Tools for life and independence

items.title: Rights Assistance and Support with Authorities

items.title: Community, Belonging, and Social Connection

items.title: Housing Support and Foster Families
items.text: Assistance in finding housing solutions, guidance for foster families, and support throughout adoption processes — creating a stable and secure home.

yatomNet.title: Claiming rights starts from the file, not from the family
yatomNet.text: Many of the rights orphans are entitled to go unclaimed, because families have to know what exists, what to look for and whom to approach. Yatom-Net is a case-file system that identifies which rights may be relevant based on the data in the child's file – and shows what can already be claimed.

statistics.title: Orphanhood Statistics in Israel – 2025
statistics.intro: Official data on orphanhood in Israel, based on publications by the Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS).
meaning: The data indicates that orphanhood in Israel is not a marginal phenomenon and affects tens of thousands of families.
The scope includes children, adolescents, and young adults, highlighting that coping with orphanhood does not end at the age of 18.
A significant portion of orphans face poverty and complex housing conditions, in addition to the loss itself.
The figures emphasize the need for public recognition and long-term responses, rather than isolated or short-term solutions.
statistics.source: Data source: Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS), 2025
statistics.note: The data reflects a national snapshot and does not include an assessment of emotional, educational, or therapeutic needs.

story.title: The Story Behind Mishpacha
story.subtitle: A personal mission that became a social initiative

person.name: Delalin Destaw
person.role: Founder and President of Mishpacha Association

content: Delalin Destaw is a social entrepreneur, author, and a Captain in the Israel Defense Forces, driven by a deep sense of mission to support orphaned children and youth facing complex life circumstances.

Delalin lost both of his parents at a young age. He immigrated to Israel 13 years ago with his uncle, grew up in Afula, and now lives in Tel Aviv. His personal life story lies at the heart of the association’s founding, and from lived experience emerged the decision to act so that no child would ever feel alone.

During his service in the IDF, Delalin served in the Education and Youth Corps and later in the Civil Administration and COGAT, holding leadership and educational roles in both routine and emergency situations, guided by the belief that leadership means seeing the person behind the uniform.

Mishpacha Association operates from a community-based approach, offering long-term accompaniment and genuine human connections, and leads a shift in perception from 'at-risk youth' to 'youth with potential', grounded in a deep belief in people and in the ability to grow even from complex realities.

Delalin is the author of the book "Running the Long Distance", an autobiographical and values-driven work that provides inspiration and practical tools for young people and individuals at life crossroads. He is a graduate of the National Student and Youth Council, a recipient of the Minister of Education’s Award for Youth Volunteering, and was selected as one of Israel’s 20 most influential young leaders.
story.closing: The work of Mishpacha and Delalin’s personal journey are united by one simple belief and one clear vision: every child deserves a Mishpacha, and every person deserves an opportunity.

orphanWeek.title: Israeli Orphans’ Families Week
orphanWeek.intro: A national week dedicated to placing the issue of orphanhood at the center of educational, community, and public discourse – grounded in recognition, responsibility, and resilience.
orphanWeek.aboutToggle: Click for a full explanation of the week
aboutText: In Israel, thousands of children, adolescents, and young adults have lost a parent, yet the experience of orphanhood often remains invisible and excluded from public discourse. Israeli Orphans’ Families Week was created to change this – not out of pity, but out of recognition of the lived reality of orphans and the shared responsibility of society as a whole to accompany, support, and include them.

The week creates an educational, community, and national continuum: safe dialogue in schools, increased public awareness, policy advancement, and community support – with the aim of strengthening visibility, belonging, and resilience for orphaned families and for Israeli society as a whole.

days.label: Sunday – Opening and Recognition
days.title: National Opening Event
days.text: The opening day is dedicated to public and official recognition of the lived reality of orphaned children and adolescents. It marks the placement of the issue at the center of public attention through personal testimonies, remarks by education and welfare professionals, and public representatives, alongside a call for sustained social responsibility.

days.label: Monday–Wednesday – Education and Awareness
days.title: Educational Dialogue and Raising Awareness
days.text: These days are devoted to educational and community-based work: lesson plans in schools, age-appropriate classroom discussions, community activities, and media exposure. The emphasis is on understanding, empathy, and providing tools for becoming a supportive society – without pity and without silencing.

days.label: Thursday – Policy and Responsibility
days.title: Advancing Policy and Rights
days.text: This day focuses on the systemic dimensions of orphanhood: meetings with government ministries, local authorities, and professional stakeholders, aimed at advancing recognition, rights, and sustained support frameworks for orphaned children and adults.

days.label: Friday–Saturday – Community and Belonging
days.title: Community Activities and Strengthening Belonging
days.text: The closing of the week is dedicated to the community: gatherings, cultural activities, and events that strengthen connection, visibility, and belonging, and emphasize that orphanhood is not loneliness – but a lived reality that can and must be accompanied together.

orphanWeek.note: Israeli Orphans’ Families Week is a first step in an ongoing process of educational, social, and systemic change – for orphans and for a more sensitive, responsible, and inclusive society.

accessibility.title: Accessibility Statement

Mishpacha Association is committed to providing an accessible experience for all users, including people with disabilities.

  • Full keyboard navigation
  • Improved compatibility with screen readers
  • Readable text and appropriate contrast

Limitations

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.html:
Mishpacha Association respects users' privacy and acts in accordance with applicable Israeli law.

Information we collect

We may collect personal information that users provide voluntarily, such as name, email address, and message content.

We use the information to respond to inquiries, contact users, operate the association’s activities, and improve user experience. We do not share personal data with third parties unless required by law.
